# More Than a Hack 2027 — Phase 1 technical document

**Team:** `Tiki-Data` — Martim Coelho, Guilherme Valido, Gonçalo Neves
**Repository:** `https://github.com/coelho121/more-than-a-hack`
**Submission file:** `Tiki-Data.csv`, regenerated by `python scripts/make_submission.py --name Tiki-Data`

---

## 1. Approach in one paragraph

A rule-based, fully deterministic pipeline with no trained model. It answers two separate
questions for every frame of the tactical video: **is the ball dead?** (`src/dead_ball.py`) and,
if it is alive, **which team has controlled possession?** (`src/possession.py`). Every rule is a
statement about football that would apply to any match, every threshold is a named constant with
its justification written next to it, and nothing in the code refers to a specific frame of this
game. We chose rules over a learned model because the provided game cannot be used for training
or tuning, there is no leaderboard, and a method whose every decision can be read and argued
about seemed the most honest use of three days.

The baseline treats "the tracker lost the ball" as dead ball and takes a majority vote of the
nearest player. Its two failures drove our design: it invents hundreds of short possessions
(594, of which 229 last under 3 s) and it has no real notion of a stoppage.

## 2. Assets used

| Asset | Used? | How |
|---|---|---|
| Tactical ATD (players + ball) | Yes | Core input: ball position, distances to players, player speeds |
| Smart Tagging | Marginally | Only the two `Kick Off (Start)` set pieces, to locate the kick-off inside each half |
| Tactical video | Not as input | Watched by the team to understand the data and debug rules (see §7) |
| Homography, broadcast video, broadcast ATD | No | Out of scope for the time available |

**Tried and dropped**

- *Smart Tagging set pieces as stoppage detectors.* The set-piece intervals are fixed windows
  (35 s, or 5 s for kick-offs) that start around the restart, so they do not tell when a
  stoppage begins or how long it lasts. We use them only as an independent sanity check in
  `scripts/report.py`.
- *Smart Tagging goals.* The file has four `Kick Off (After Goal)` tags and four `GOALS` tags
  for a match with three goals, so at least one is a false positive. The goal rule built on
  them is still in the code but adds zero frames on this match: the stoppages after goals are
  already found by the ball-gap rules. We did not remove the false tag by hand.
- *The ball speed column of the ATD.* Its 99th percentile is under 6 m/s, which is not a ball.
  We compute displacement from positions instead.
- *"Ball not visible = dead ball."* Our first reading of the gap statistics. The one definition
  check we ran on the public ground truth (§7) showed it is wrong in both directions.
- *Player speed to find the whistle before the ball disappears.* Players slow down gradually
  over several seconds; there is no usable instant.
- *Identifying which team takes each restart.* Small expected gain, real risk to a stable part.

## 3. Dead-ball rules (`src/dead_ball.py`)

A frame is `D` in six situations. The union is then cleaned with two football constraints: no
stoppage shorter than 2 s and no live play shorter than 2 s between two stoppages.

1. **Before the kick-off of each half.** Inside the tagged kick-off interval, the kick-off is
   the moment the ball leaves a 1.5 m circle around the centre spot (fallback: middle of the
   interval). Detected at +3 and −20 frames from the two published kick-off frames.
2. **Ball seen more than 0.5 m outside the pitch.**
3. **Ball gaps** (runs of at least 2 s with no ball position; there are 133). The ball
   disappears when it leaves the pitch, when someone picks it up, or when it is occluded.
   Questions are asked in order and the first "yes" decides:

   | | Question | Decision |
   |---|---|---|
   | a | Gap touches the start or end of the half? | D |
   | b | Ball last seen within 2 m of a boundary line? | D |
   | c | Ball heading out (position + velocity over 1 s)? | D |
   | d | Ball reappears within 2 m of a boundary line? | D |
   | e | Gap longer than 15 s? | D |
   | f | Outside both penalty areas and players walking (collective speed < 1.5 m/s)? | D |
   | g | Outside both penalty areas and players running? | alive, possession is held |
   | h | Otherwise: short and in a penalty area (goalkeeper holding the ball) | alive, possession is held |

   "Collective speed" is the median speed of the tracked players in a frame, averaged over the
   gap. The 1.5 m/s limit is walking pace; `scripts/speed_diagnostic.py` shows it separates gaps
   where the ball certainly went out (median 1.15 m/s) from open play (median 2.0 m/s) with about
   20% error each way. Both reference groups are defined by the other rules, not by any label.
4. **Ball visible but at rest** (stays within 1 m for a full second). It is `D` if it is adjacent
   to another stoppage, or at rest for 3 s with no player within 2 m for at least 1 s (ball placed
   for a free kick, corner or goal kick), or at rest for 8 s. The stoppage ends when the ball
   leaves its resting spot.
5. **Goals**, from `Kick Off (After Goal)` tags. Inert on this match (§2).
6. **False play inside a stoppage.** A stretch of "live play" between two detected stoppages that
   lasts under 7 s while the players are walking is players returning the ball, not play. Speed
   is never used alone: slow build-up is not flanked by stoppages, and a throw-in that goes
   straight out again has players running. Before this rule, 17 of the 19 inter-stoppage
   stretches under 5 s were at walking pace, against 0 of the 31 stretches over 40 s.

## 4. Possession rules (`src/possession.py`)

The challenge asks for *controlled* possession: a touch, a deflection or an aerial duel does not
change it, and a loose ball stays with the last team.

1. **Control in a frame.** A team controls the ball if its nearest player is within 1.8 m of the
   ball and at least 0.3 m closer than the nearest opponent. If both are on the ball, or nobody
   is within reach (a pass in flight), nobody controls and possession is unchanged.
2. **Touches and sequences.** Consecutive control frames of one team form a touch (minimum 3
   frames). Consecutive touches of the same team with no opponent touch in between form a
   sequence. A sequence is controlled possession only if it accumulates **0.6 s** of control.
   Clearances, deflections and a ball passing near an opponent are dropped.
3. **Back-dating.** Possession changes at the *start* of the valid sequence, not when it is
   confirmed. The match is processed offline, and `spellF1` is harsh on lag.
4. **Minimum duration.** A possession shorter than **2 s** between two possessions of the
   opponent is removed. The first and last possession of each live stretch are kept.
5. **Restarts.** After every stoppage possession starts fresh: from the restart to the first
   valid sequence, the ball belongs to that sequence's team.

While the ball is hidden but play continues (gap rules g and h) there are no touches, so
possession is held, as the challenge prescribes for loose and contested balls.

## 5. How the parameters were chosen

No parameter was tuned on the provided game or on the public ground truth.

- **Dead-ball parameters:** football reasoning plus aggregate statistics of the whole match that
  involve no label (gap lengths, distance distributions, player speeds).
- **Possession parameters:** football reasoning, then checked on *other games* (§6).
- **Sensitivity** (`scripts/sensitivity.py`): each parameter is moved ±30% and the output is
  compared with our own default using the official `spellF1`. All dead-ball parameters stay at
  0.96 or above, so none sits at a fragile point. The possession parameters are the sensitive
  ones (0.85–0.94 for the control radius, control time and minimum duration), which is why they
  are the ones we validated externally.

## 6. External data

No model was trained, so there is no training set. One external dataset was used for validation:

- **What:** Metrica Sports public sample data, Sample Game 1 and Sample Game 2 (anonymised
  matches, tracking at 25 fps and event data). <https://github.com/metrica-sports/sample-data>
- **Labels:** the event annotations published by Metrica with that data. We labelled nothing.
- **How it was used** (`scripts/external_validation.py`): we derive a reference possession from
  the events (dead ball = no ball in the tracking for 1 s or more; team = team of the last
  possession event), run our possession rules with that reference dead ball, and score with the
  official `spellF1`. Two variants of the reference and two noise levels were used.
- **Result:** the control radius barely matters between 1.0 and 3.0 m; shorter control time and
  shorter minimum duration agree better with event-based possession. We moved from our initial
  1.0 s / 3 s to **0.6 s / 2 s** (0.59 → 0.63 and 0.64 → 0.67 on the two references). We did not
  go to the optimum of that study (near 0 s) because the event-based reference counts more short
  possessions than the challenge definition, and the sample tracking is cleaner than the ATD.

## 7. What the public ground truth and the video were used for

- **Pipeline correctness.** `scripts/check_reproduces_baseline.py` confirms that our data loading,
  frame alignment and CSV writing reproduce `baseline_smooth50.csv` exactly. The public-window
  score is printed by our scripts as an alarm for broken code only.
- **One definition check, run once** (`scripts/definition_check.py`): a 3×2 table crossing the
  public label with "is the ball visible?", to learn what "dead" means in the reference, as
  CHALLENGE.md invites. It showed that an invisible ball is not reliably dead and that most dead
  ball has the ball visible. No number from it entered the code.
- **Never** used to choose between versions or to set a threshold. Two of our changes lowered
  the public-window score and were kept, because the reasons for them came from elsewhere.
- **Video.** Team members watched samples of moments printed by `scripts/moments.py` to
  understand failure patterns (for example the "false play inside a stoppage" pattern of rule 6).
  No labels, corrections or frame-specific constants came out of it; each observation was turned
  into a general rule or left as a limitation.
- **LLM use.** An LLM assistant (Claude) helped write the code and this document. The tracking,
  Smart Tagging and video files were never uploaded to it; the work was driven by error messages
  and aggregate statistics.

## 8. Result on the provided game (no ground truth involved)

| | `baseline_smooth50` | Ours |
|---|---|---|
| Possessions | 594 | 258 |
| Possessions under 3 s | 229 | 38 |
| Mean possession | 7.2 s | 13.4 s |
| Possessions over 60 s | 1 | 0 |
| Live time | 71.7 min | 57.7 min |
| Stoppages | 133 | 94 |
| Possessions per half | 303 / 291 | 135 / 123 |

Frames outside the two halves are `X`. `scripts/check_deterministic.py` generates the file twice
in separate processes and compares SHA-256 hashes.

## 9. Limitations and what we would do with more time

- **Stoppage boundaries when the ball stays visible.** After the whistle players often keep
  touching the ball before someone picks it up, and after the ball comes back they may pass it
  around before the real restart. We only fix this when it happens *between* two detected
  stoppages. This is probably our largest remaining error; a whistle detector from the broadcast
  audio or from referee tracks would be the next thing to try.
- **Who takes the restart.** If the restarting team loses the ball within a second or two, we
  give the whole stretch to the opponent.
- **Short possessions that end in a stoppage** with less than 0.6 s of control are missed.
- **No height.** A ball flying over a player looks like a ball at his feet; the control-time
  rule filters most of it.
- **Gap rules b–d and f are heuristics.** A winger shielding the ball on the touchline while the
  camera loses it is labelled dead; about one in five decisions of rule f is expected to be wrong.
- **Goalkeeper holds** are recognised by position only (rule h).
- **Smart Tagging and broadcast data are almost unused.** The tagged phases carry a team and
  could support possession during hidden-ball stretches.
- **Validated on two external games only**, with an event-derived reference that is not the
  challenge's definition.

## 10. Reproduction

Python 3.12, dependencies pinned in `requirements.txt`.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate                  # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
# unpack the match bundle into data/ (see docs/oficial/DATA.md), or set MTAH_DATA_DIR
python scripts/make_submission.py --name Tiki-Data
```

This writes and validates `evaluation/results/Tiki-Data.csv`. The first run builds a cache of
the tracking in `cache/` (1–2 minutes). The same code and data always produce the same bytes.

Optional checks: `scripts/check_reproduces_baseline.py`, `scripts/check_deterministic.py`,
`scripts/report.py`, `scripts/sensitivity.py`, `scripts/speed_diagnostic.py`, and
`scripts/external_validation.py` (needs
`git clone https://github.com/metrica-sports/sample-data external/sample-data`).
